lessons.title: Animal, plant and bacterial cells
lessons.summary: Nuclei contain genetic material; ribosomes make proteins; mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Nuclei contain genetic material; ribosomes make proteins; mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration. Cytoplasm supports many reactions and membranes control movement. Photosynthetic plant cells also have chloroplasts, cellulose walls and a permanent vacuole.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Bacteria have a membrane, wall, cytoplasm and ribosomes but no nucleus. Their main DNA forms a loop; plasmids are extra DNA rings. Underground root hair cells normally lack chloroplasts, so do not draw every plant cell as a photosynthetic leaf cell.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Eukaryotic or prokaryotic? Animal and plant cells are eukaryotic: their genetic material is enclosed in a nucleus. Bacteria are prokaryotic: they are much smaller (often 1–10 μm against 10–100 μm) and their DNA is a single loop plus plasmids. Some bacteria also have flagella for movement.

Order of magnitude. If a plant cell is 100 μm wide and a bacterium is 1 μm wide, the plant cell is 10² times wider: two orders of magnitude. In exam answers, link each structure to its job, for example: "chloroplasts absorb light for photosynthesis", not just "has chloroplasts".

keypoints: Nuclei contain genetic material; ribosomes make proteins; mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration.
Bacteria have a membrane, wall, cytoplasm and ribosomes but no nucleus.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Which structure makes proteins?
Where is the main bacterial DNA?
Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
checks.why: Plant cells have cellulose cell walls; animal cells do not.

checks.q: What is a plasmid?
opts: A small ring of DNA in a bacterium
checks.why: Plasmids are small extra rings of DNA found in many bacteria.

checks.q: Bacteria are described as prokaryotic because…
opts: their genetic material is not in a nucleus

checks.q: Which organelle releases most of the energy from aerobic respiration?
checks.why: Aerobic respiration takes place mainly in mitochondria.

exam.q: Explain three differences between a typical photosynthetic plant cell and a bacterial cell.
ms: Plant DNA is enclosed in a nucleus; bacterial DNA is not.
The plant cell has chloroplasts; the bacterium does not.
The plant cell has a permanent vacuole; the bacterium does not.

exam.q: A cell is 50 μm across. A bacterium is 0.5 μm across. Calculate how many orders of magnitude larger the cell is.
ms: 100 = 10², so two orders of magnitude.

exam.q: Describe the functions of four structures found in a palisade leaf cell.
ms: Nucleus contains genetic material that controls the cell.
Chloroplasts absorb light for photosynthesis.
Cellulose cell wall strengthens/supports the cell.
Permanent vacuole contains cell sap / keeps the cell turgid. Accept mitochondria for respiration, ribosomes for protein synthesis, membrane controls movement of substances.

example.title: Comparing sizes
example.q: A plant cell is 0.08 mm wide. A bacterium is 2 μm long. How many times larger is the plant cell?
steps: Give it as a ratio, with no unit.
The plant cell is 40 times larger (just over one order of magnitude).

lessons.title: Microscopy and magnification
lessons.summary: Magnification enlarges an image; resolution distinguishes close points.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Magnification enlarges an image; resolution distinguishes close points. Electron microscopes reveal finer detail than light microscopes because they have greater resolution as well as greater magnification. Enlarging a blurry image does not reveal new detail.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Convert units before dividing: 1 mm = 1000 μm. A 36 mm image representing a 12 μm cell has magnification 36000 ÷ 12 = 3000. Magnification has no unit.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Rearranging the equation. The magnification triangle gives three forms: magnification = image ÷ real, real = image ÷ magnification, image = real × magnification. Always convert both lengths to the same unit first.

Units ladder. 1 m = 1000 mm; 1 mm = 1000 μm; 1 μm = 1000 nm. Very small sizes are often written in standard form: 0.000 002 m = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m.

Why electron microscopes changed biology. Their greater resolution revealed ribosomes, the internal membranes of mitochondria and chloroplasts, and viruses. This improved our understanding of subcellular structures. Light microscopes can, however, view living cells and colours.

keypoints: Magnification enlarges an image; resolution distinguishes close points.
Magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: A 20 μm cell appears 40 mm long. Calculate magnification.
What distinguishes two close organelles?
An image is 12 mm long. The real object is 0.03 mm long. What is the magnification?
How many micrometres are in 1 mm?
Which of these can only be seen clearly with an electron microscope?
checks.why: Ribosomes are too small to resolve with a light microscope.

checks.q: Write 0.000 005 m in standard form.
checks.why: Move the decimal point 6 places: 5 × 10⁻⁶ m.

exam.q: A cell image is 54 mm wide at ×1800. Calculate actual width in micrometres.
ms: Actual size = image size / magnification.

exam.q: A student draws a cheek cell 60 mm wide. The real cell is 60 μm wide. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
Compare light microscopes and electron microscopes. Explain how electron microscopy has improved our understanding of cells.
ms: Electron microscopes have higher magnification.
Electron microscopes have higher resolution / can distinguish two points closer together.
So smaller subcellular structures (e.g. ribosomes, internal structure of mitochondria/chloroplasts) can be seen.
Light microscopes are cheaper/portable and can view living specimens in colour.

practical.title: Required practical 1 · Light microscopy
method: Place a thin plant tissue layer on a slide, add suitable stain and lower a coverslip at an angle.
Start on low power and focus with coarse then fine adjustment; increase power as appropriate.
Observe plant and prepared animal cells; make clear proportional labelled drawings with a scale or magnification.
variables: Keep specimen thickness and illumination suitable.
Record eyepiece and objective magnifications.
safety: Handle glass slides carefully.
Avoid stain contact and follow school eye-protection guidance.
practical.analysis: Use image size divided by magnification for actual size, with consistent units. Total microscope magnification equals eyepiece × objective.

example.title: Real size from an image
example.q: A mitochondrion appears 30 mm long in an electron micrograph at × 15 000. Calculate its real length in μm.
steps: Keep the unit of the image.

lessons.title: Specialisation and differentiation
lessons.summary: Differentiation develops specialised structures.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Differentiation develops specialised structures. Most animal cells differentiate early; many plant cells retain this ability throughout life. Mature animal cell division mainly supports repair and replacement. Explain why a feature suits a task rather than merely listing features.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Sperm have a tail for swimming and many mitochondria. Nerve cells have long extensions for impulse transmission; muscle cells have contractile proteins. Root hairs enlarge absorbing area. Hollow lignified xylem conducts water; living phloem transports sugars.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Structure → function chains. Strong answers use "feature, so, therefore": a root hair cell has a long extension, so it has a large surface area, therefore water and mineral ions are absorbed faster.

Five cells to know. Sperm (tail, many mitochondria, acrosome enzymes to digest the egg coat, haploid nucleus); nerve cell (long axon, branched dendrites to connect); muscle cell (protein fibres that contract, many mitochondria); root hair cell (large area, no chloroplasts); xylem and phloem (see Plant tissues).

Differentiation. As a cell differentiates it gains new subcellular structures. In mature animals cell division is mainly for repair and replacement, whereas plant meristems keep producing new specialised cells.

keypoints: Differentiation develops specialised structures.
Sperm have a tail for swimming and many mitochondria.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: What is differentiation?
Why is a root hair useful?
Why does a sperm cell contain many mitochondria?
opts: To store food for the embryo
To release energy for the tail to swim
checks.why: Respiration in mitochondria releases energy for swimming.

checks.q: Why do root hair cells usually lack chloroplasts?
opts: They are underground and receive no light
checks.why: No light reaches roots, so chloroplasts would be no use.

checks.q: Which describes differentiation?
opts: A cell divides into two identical cells
A cell takes in water by osmosis
A cell gains new structures to do a particular job
checks.why: Differentiation is the process of a cell becoming specialised.

checks.q: What do the branched dendrites of a nerve cell do?
opts: Connect with many other nerve cells
checks.why: Branched endings let a neurone receive impulses from many cells.

exam.q: Explain three adaptations of a sperm cell for fertilisation.
ms: A tail allows movement towards an egg.
Many mitochondria support respiration for movement.
Enzymes in the head help penetrate egg coverings.

exam.q: Explain why most animal cells lose the ability to differentiate, while many plant cells keep it.
ms: Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage; in adults division is mainly for repair/replacement.
Plants have meristems / continue growing throughout life, so they keep producing new specialised cells.

exam.q: Describe how a nerve cell and a root hair cell are each adapted to their function.
ms: Nerve cell has a long axon to carry impulses over long distances.
Nerve cell has branched endings/dendrites to connect with many cells.
Root hair cell has a long extension giving a large surface area.
For absorbing water and mineral ions (faster) / many mitochondria for active transport.

example.title: Writing a linked adaptation
example.q: Explain how one feature of a muscle cell helps it contract.
steps: Choose a feature you can link to energy or contraction.
Link the structure to a process.
Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, releasing energy.
Finish with the job of the cell.
This energy is needed for the protein fibres to contract.

lessons.title: Mitosis and the cell cycle
lessons.summary: Chromosomes contain DNA and many genes; body cells normally have chromosome pairs.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Chromosomes contain DNA and many genes; body cells normally have chromosome pairs. Before division, a cell grows, increases its organelles and copies its DNA. These preparations give daughter cells complete genetic information and cell machinery.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: During mitosis, chromosome copies separate and nuclei divide. Cytoplasm and membrane then divide to form two genetically identical cells with the original chromosome number. Mitosis supports growth and repair, whereas meiosis forms gametes.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
The three stages of the cell cycle. (1) Growth and DNA replication: the cell grows, makes more ribosomes and mitochondria, and copies each chromosome. (2) Mitosis: one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides. (3) Cytokinesis: the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to form two identical daughter cells.

Chromosome numbers. A human body cell has 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). After mitosis, each daughter cell still has 46. Doubling questions use powers of two: after n cycles, one cell gives 2ⁿ cells.

Interpreting a cell-cycle chart. The fraction of cells seen in a stage is proportional to the time spent in it. If 10 of 200 cells are in mitosis and the cycle lasts 20 hours, mitosis lasts about (10 ÷ 200) × 20 = 1 hour.

keypoints: Chromosomes contain DNA and many genes; body cells normally have chromosome pairs.
During mitosis, chromosome copies separate and nuclei divide.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Three cells each complete two rounds of division. How many result?
What happens before mitosis?
How many chromosomes are in a human skin cell after mitosis?
checks.why: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same.

checks.q: Why must DNA be copied before mitosis?
opts: So the cell can grow a cell wall
So each daughter cell receives a full set of chromosomes
checks.why: Each new cell needs complete genetic information.

checks.q: Which is NOT a use of mitosis?
One cell divides by mitosis five times. How many cells result?

exam.q: Describe how the cell cycle produces two genetically identical daughter cells.
ms: DNA is replicated before division.
Copies of each chromosome separate to opposite ends and nuclei divide.
Cytoplasm and membrane divide, leaving identical chromosome sets.

exam.q: Give two ways a cell prepares for division before mitosis.
ms: It grows / increases the number of subcellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria.
It copies/replicates its DNA so each chromosome forms two copies.

exam.q: A scientist counts cells in an onion root tip: 380 cells not dividing and 20 cells in mitosis. The cell cycle takes 24 hours. Calculate the time spent in mitosis in minutes, and explain why the root tip is a good place to look.
ms: Total cells = 400.
= 72 minutes.
Root tips contain meristem cells that divide frequently.

example.title: Time in mitosis
example.q: In a root tip, 24 of 400 cells are dividing. The full cycle takes 16 hours. Estimate how long mitosis takes.
steps: The proportion of cells equals the proportion of time.

lessons.title: Stem cells: benefits, risks and ethics
lessons.summary: Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can divide and differentiate.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can divide and differentiate. Embryonic stem cells can form most human cell types; adult bone-marrow stem cells produce a more limited range, including blood cells. Plant meristems can produce different plant tissues throughout life.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Replacement cells may help damaged tissues, but infection and uncontrolled division are risks. Therapeutic cloning produces genetically matched cells, reducing rejection. Embryo use raises ethical objections. Meristems can rapidly clone rare plants or crops with desirable characteristics.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Three sources. Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into almost any cell type. Adult stem cells from bone marrow form a limited range, such as blood cells. Plant meristem cells, found in root and shoot tips, can form any plant tissue.

Therapeutic cloning. A patient's body cell nucleus is transferred into an enucleated egg cell; the embryo produced supplies stem cells with the patient's genes, so they are not rejected.

Evaluating. A balanced evaluation gives benefits (treating diabetes or paralysis, no rejection with matched cells), risks (viral contamination, tumour formation), ethical issues (destruction of embryos, consent) and a justified conclusion. Plant cloning from meristems is quick and cheap, protects rare species and gives crops with known traits, but the clones share the same disease vulnerability.

keypoints: Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can divide and differentiate.
Replacement cells may help damaged tissues, but infection and uncontrolled division are risks.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Where are adult human stem cells found?
Why use genetically matched stem cells?
Where are meristems found in a plant?
checks.why: Meristems are regions of active cell division at root and shoot tips.

checks.q: What is the main advantage of therapeutic cloning?
opts: Stem cells match the patient so are not rejected
checks.why: The cells have the patient's genes.

checks.q: Which is a risk of stem-cell treatment?
opts: Cells are too large to inject

checks.q: Which cell type can adult bone marrow stem cells form?
checks.why: Bone marrow stem cells produce a limited range, including blood cells.

exam.q: Evaluate embryonic stem cells for replacing damaged nerve tissue.
ms: They can differentiate into a wider range of cell types than many adult stem cells.
A biological risk such as infection or uncontrolled division must be considered.
Potential treatment benefit must be weighed against ethical concerns about embryo use.

exam.q: Describe how plant meristem tissue can be used to save a rare plant species from extinction.
ms: Meristem cells are removed from root/shoot tip.
Grown on a medium/in sterile conditions to form many clones.
Clones are identical, quickly produced and can be replanted/stored.

exam.q: Stem cells from embryos could be used to treat type 1 diabetes. Evaluate this use of stem cells.
ms: Stem cells could be differentiated into insulin-producing pancreas cells.
This could cure the condition / remove the need for insulin injections.
Therapeutic cloning gives cells that are not rejected by the immune system.
Risk of transferring viral infection from cultured cells.
Risk of cells dividing uncontrollably / tumours.
Ethical/religious objections to using embryos, with a justified conclusion.

example.title: Structuring an evaluation
example.q: Evaluate using cloned meristem tissue to produce banana plants.
steps: Many identical plants produced quickly and cheaply.
Plants keep desirable features, such as high yield.
All the plants are genetically identical, so one disease could destroy the whole crop.
Useful for rapid supply, but growers should keep some genetic variety or use disease control.

lessons.title: Diffusion and exchange surfaces
lessons.summary: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient. Higher temperature, larger area and a steeper gradient usually increase its rate. Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross cell membranes by diffusion; the process itself requires no energy from respiration.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: As size increases, surface area to volume ratio decreases. Large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems. Alveoli and villi have large areas and short diffusion distances; blood flow and ventilation maintain gradients.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Surface area to volume ratio. For a cube of side L: area = 6L², volume = L³, so SA:V = 6 ÷ L. A 1 cm cube has 6:1; a 3 cm cube has 2:1. Single-celled organisms have a large SA:V, so diffusion across their membrane is enough.

Effective exchange surfaces have a large surface area, a thin membrane or short diffusion path, an efficient blood supply (animals) and ventilation (gas exchange). Examples: alveoli in lungs, villi in the small intestine, gills (filaments and lamellae with counter-current blood flow), and root hairs and leaves in plants.

Fick's idea. Rate of diffusion ∝ surface area × concentration difference ÷ thickness of membrane. Doubling the area doubles the rate; doubling the thickness halves it.

keypoints: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient.
As size increases, surface area to volume ratio decreases.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: A cube has side 2 cm. Express its surface area to volume ratio as x:1.
Which change speeds diffusion?
What is the SA:V of a 3 cm cube?
How do fish gills maintain a steep concentration gradient?
opts: Blood flows in the opposite direction to water
checks.why: Counter-current flow keeps a gradient along the whole gill.

checks.q: Which change would halve the rate of diffusion across a membrane?
checks.why: Rate is inversely proportional to the diffusion distance.

checks.q: Why do single-celled organisms not need a gas exchange system?
opts: They have a large surface area to volume ratio
They are too small to need oxygen
checks.why: Diffusion across the membrane meets their needs.

exam.q: Explain why alveoli exchange gases rapidly.
ms: Many alveoli provide a large surface area.
Thin walls give a short diffusion distance.
Ventilation and blood flow maintain concentration gradients.

exam.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube of side 5 mm. Give your answer as a ratio x : 1.
ms: Surface area = 6 × 25 = 150 mm².
Volume = 125 mm³.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of villi in the small intestine increases the rate of absorption of digested food.
ms: Villi (and microvilli) give a large surface area.
Wall is one cell thick / short diffusion distance.
Rich capillary network carries absorbed molecules away.
Which maintains a steep concentration gradient. Accept many mitochondria for active transport.

example.title: Comparing SA:V
example.q: Compare the SA:V of a 1 cm cube and a 4 cm cube.
steps: Larger objects have a smaller ratio.
The larger cube has a quarter of the SA:V, so it would need an exchange surface or transport system.

lessons.title: Osmosis and percentage mass change
lessons.summary: Osmosis is net water movement through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Osmosis is net water movement through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution. Water moves both ways, but there is a net movement when concentrations differ. Water entry can make plant cells turgid.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Percentage mass change = (final − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100. Changing from 2.0 g to 2.3 g gives +15%; a negative value means loss. A graph crossing zero estimates a solution concentration causing no net water movement.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Animal and plant cells respond differently. In pure water, an animal cell gains water and may burst because it has no cell wall. A plant cell swells until the wall pushes back and it becomes turgid. In a concentrated solution, plant cells lose water and become flaccid; the membrane may pull away from the wall (plasmolysis).

Reading the graph. Plot percentage change in mass against concentration. Where the line crosses 0% there is no net movement, so the solution has the same water concentration as the cell contents. Percentage change is used rather than mass change because starting masses differ.

Improving the practical. Blot cylinders dry in the same way, use the same cork borer and length, repeat at each concentration and calculate a mean.

keypoints: Osmosis is net water movement through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution.
Percentage mass change = (final − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: A cylinder changes from 4.0 g to 3.6 g. Calculate percentage mass change.
When does water enter a cell by osmosis?
opts: Outside is more dilute than inside
checks.why: Outside is more dilute than inside

checks.q: A potato piece goes from 2.50 g to 2.00 g. What is the percentage change?
Why might a red blood cell burst in pure water?
opts: It gains water by osmosis and has no cell wall
checks.why: Animal cells have no wall to resist swelling.

checks.q: Why is percentage change in mass calculated rather than change in mass?
opts: It removes the need for repeats
The pieces had different starting masses

checks.q: What describes a plant cell that has lost a lot of water?
checks.why: Cells that lose water become flaccid.

exam.q: Explain why potato tissue loses mass in concentrated sugar solution.
ms: The outside solution is more concentrated than the cell contents.
Water moves out by osmosis across partially permeable cell membranes.
Water loss reduces tissue mass.

exam.q: Explain why potato cylinders should be blotted dry before reweighing.
ms: Removes surface solution/water.
So the mass measured is only that of the tissue / measurements are comparable.

exam.q: Describe a method to find the concentration of sucrose solution with the same water concentration as potato cells.
ms: Cut potato cylinders of the same size/with the same borer and length.
Blot and weigh each cylinder.
Place in a range of sucrose concentrations, e.g. 0 to 1.0 mol/dm³.
Leave for the same time at the same temperature.
Remove, blot dry in the same way and reweigh; calculate percentage change.
Plot % change against concentration; where the line crosses zero is the answer.

practical.title: Required practical 3 · Osmosis in plant tissue
method: Cut equal potato cylinders and record initial masses.
Immerse in equal volumes of a concentration range for equal times.
Remove, blot consistently and reweigh; repeat each concentration.
variables: Independent: sugar or salt concentration.
Dependent: percentage mass change.
Control dimensions, tissue source, solution volume, temperature and time.
safety: Use cutting equipment on a suitable surface under supervision.
Do not eat laboratory samples.
practical.analysis: Calculate percentage changes and means. Plot concentration against percentage change and interpolate the zero-change concentration, recognising scatter and measurement uncertainty.

example.title: Finding the 'no change' concentration
example.q: Percentage mass change was +8% at 0.2 mol/dm³ and −4% at 0.4 mol/dm³. Assuming a straight line, estimate where change is zero.

lessons.title: Active transport and comparing transport
lessons.summary: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration. It requires energy from respiration. Root hairs absorb mineral ions from dilute soil solutions; intestinal cells can absorb sugars against their gradient.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Diffusion moves particles down a gradient; osmosis specifically describes water through a partially permeable membrane; active transport needs energy. Many mitochondria can support energy-demanding transport. The presence of a membrane alone does not prove osmosis: identify the substance moving.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Carrier proteins and energy. In active transport, carrier proteins in the membrane pick up particles and move them across using energy released from respiration. Cells that do a lot of active transport, like root hair cells and cells lining the gut, contain many mitochondria.

Why plants need it. Mineral ions such as nitrate (for proteins) and magnesium (for chlorophyll) are usually more concentrated inside root cells than in the soil, so diffusion would move them the wrong way.

Comparison table. Diffusion: down a gradient, passive, any small particle. Osmosis: water only, down its gradient, through a partially permeable membrane, passive. Active transport: against a gradient, needs energy, uses carrier proteins.

keypoints: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration.
Diffusion moves particles down a gradient; osmosis specifically describes water through a partially permeable membrane; active transport needs energy.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Which process requires energy from respiration?
Mineral concentration is lower in soil than a root cell. Uptake uses…
What do carrier proteins do in active transport?
opts: Move particles across the membrane using energy
checks.why: Carrier proteins transport substances against the gradient.

checks.q: Why do plants need nitrate ions?
checks.why: Nitrate supplies nitrogen for amino acids and proteins.

checks.q: Glucose is absorbed from the gut when its concentration in the gut is lower than in the blood. This uses…
checks.why: Movement against the gradient requires active transport.

checks.q: Which process involves water moving through a partially permeable membrane?

exam.q: Explain why low oxygen availability can reduce mineral uptake by roots.
ms: Less oxygen reduces aerobic respiration.
Less energy is available for active transport.
Mineral ions need to move against their concentration gradient.

exam.q: Give two differences between diffusion and active transport.
ms: Diffusion is down a concentration gradient; active transport is against it.
Diffusion is passive/needs no energy; active transport needs energy from respiration. Accept active transport uses carrier proteins.

exam.q: Waterlogged soil contains little oxygen. Explain why plants in waterlogged soil may show signs of mineral deficiency.
ms: Root cells receive less oxygen.
So less aerobic respiration / less energy released.
Active transport of mineral ions needs energy.
So fewer mineral ions (e.g. nitrate/magnesium) are absorbed against the gradient.

example.title: Interpreting data
example.q: Root uptake of nitrate fell by 80% when a respiratory poison was added. Explain this result.
steps: Nitrate is absorbed by active transport.
Less energy is released in the root cells.
Without energy, carrier proteins cannot move nitrate against its concentration gradient.

lessons.title: Culturing bacteria and inhibition zones
lessons.summary: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission. Sterile medium and equipment, brief lid opening and sterile inoculation reduce contamination. Incubating school cultures at 25°C reduces the risk of growing harmful human pathogens. Do not reopen incubated plates.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Equal discs carrying antiseptics can be compared using clear inhibition zones. Use area = πr² with radius half the diameter. Keep disc size, agar depth, bacterial species and incubation conditions constant. A clear zone indicates inhibited growth, not necessarily that every cell was killed.

notes.title: Growth calculations
notes.html: If each bacterium divides once every 30 minutes under specified ideal conditions, a culture starting with 100 bacteria reaches 100 × 2⁴ = 1600 after two hours. Count the number of complete divisions before using powers of two. Real cultures eventually slow as resources fall and wastes accumulate.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Aseptic technique, step by step. Sterilise Petri dishes and agar before use (autoclave). Pass the inoculating loop through a Bunsen flame until red hot, then let it cool. Lift the lid only slightly to spread the bacteria. Secure the lid with two pieces of tape (not sealed all round, so oxygen can enter and harmful anaerobic bacteria are not encouraged). Store upside down so condensation does not drip onto the culture.

Mean division time. Number of bacteria at the end = number at start × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of divisions. For example, 30 minutes per division for 3 hours gives n = 6, so 1 bacterium becomes 64. Large answers are often written in standard form.

keypoints: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission.
Equal discs carrying antiseptics can be compared using clear inhibition zones.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: A clear circle has diameter 10 mm. Use π = 3.14 to calculate area.
Why incubate school cultures at 25°C?
Why is the inoculating loop passed through a flame?
Why is the Petri dish lid taped but not sealed all round?
opts: So oxygen can enter and anaerobic pathogens are not encouraged
checks.why: Taping lets air in and prevents harmful anaerobic growth.

checks.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are produced from one after 2 hours?
How do bacteria reproduce?

exam.q: Explain three precautions in preparing a bacterial culture.
ms: Sterilise medium and equipment to remove contaminants.
Minimise lid opening to reduce airborne contamination.
Secure without fully sealing the lid and incubate at 25°C to reduce risk.

exam.q: A culture starts with 500 bacteria. The mean division time is 25 minutes. Calculate the number of bacteria after 150 minutes. Give your answer in standard form.
ms: Number of divisions = 150 ÷ 25 = 6.

exam.q: Describe how to investigate the effect of three different antiseptics on the growth of bacteria.
ms: Use sterile agar plate and spread bacteria evenly with sterile technique.
Soak paper discs of the same size in each antiseptic.
Include a control disc soaked in sterile water.
Place discs on the agar, tape lid and incubate at 25 °C.
Measure the diameter of each clear zone after a set time.
Calculate area with πr² and compare; repeat for reliable means.

practical.title: Required practical 2 · Antiseptics and bacterial growth
method: Use teacher-approved cultures and aseptic technique to inoculate sterile agar evenly.
Add equally sized discs with different antiseptics or concentrations and a solvent control.
Secure the lid without fully sealing it; incubate at 25°C and measure zones without reopening.
variables: Independent: antiseptic type or concentration, changing one at a time.
Dependent: inhibition-zone area.
Control species, agar depth, disc size, incubation time and temperature.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Similar cells form tissues, tissues form organs and organs cooperate in systems. Digestion changes large insoluble molecules into small soluble molecules. Villi provide a large absorbing area and a rich blood supply in the small intestine.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Amylase from salivary glands, pancreas and small intestine breaks starch into sugars. Proteases from stomach, pancreas and small intestine produce amino acids. Lipases from pancreas and small intestine produce glycerol and fatty acids. Liver-made bile is stored in the gall bladder, neutralises acid and emulsifies fat; it is not an enzyme.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
The route and the jobs. Mouth (teeth break food up; salivary amylase starts starch digestion) → oesophagus → stomach (hydrochloric acid kills microorganisms and gives the low pH that pepsin, a protease, needs; muscular churning) → small intestine (pancreatic enzymes and bile; absorption through villi) → large intestine (water absorbed) → rectum and anus.

Bile in two jobs. Bile is alkaline, so it neutralises stomach acid and gives the higher pH that small-intestine enzymes need. It also emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase. Neither job is catalysis, so bile is not an enzyme.

Uses of products. Glucose is used in respiration; amino acids build new proteins; glycerol and fatty acids form lipids for membranes and energy stores.

lessons.title: Enzymes, temperature and pH
lessons.summary: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins. A substrate fits an active site, products are released and the enzyme can be reused. The lock-and-key model explains specificity but is simplified. Catalysts speed reactions without being used up.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Warming initially increases collisions and rate. Above an optimum, active-site shape changes and enzymes denature; extreme pH can do the same. Cold normally slows activity without denaturing. For disappearance of a fixed substrate amount, compare relative rate using 1/time.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Why enzymes are specific. Each active site has a particular shape; only a complementary substrate fits. At high temperature, bonds holding the protein's shape break, the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits. This is denaturation and it is usually permanent.

Rate calculations. Rate = amount of product formed ÷ time, or amount of substrate used ÷ time, for example 24 cm³ of gas in 40 s gives 0.6 cm³/s. If the end-point is a time, use 1000 ÷ time or 1 ÷ time as a relative rate.

Required practical. Starch and amylase are kept at set temperatures in a water bath; drops are taken every 30 s and tested with iodine on a spotting tile. The time when iodine stays orange-brown shows when starch is gone. Change one variable, such as pH (using buffer solutions), and keep the enzyme and starch concentration and volumes the same.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Iodine turns blue-black with starch. Heated Benedict’s reagent gives a green to brick-red precipitate with reducing sugars. Biuret turns lilac with protein. Sudan III stains a lipid layer red. Use the correct test conditions; reagent colour alone without the method may mislead.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Use clean separate tubes and droppers, standardised volumes and equal heating time. A known positive checks that the test works; water is a negative control. A negative result means none was detected under those conditions, not proof that absolutely none exists.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
The four tests in full. Starch: add a few drops of iodine solution; orange-brown → blue-black. Preparing the food. Grind the food with distilled water using a pestle and mortar, then filter to get a clear solution. Safety: Biuret contains copper sulfate and sodium hydroxide (irritant); ethanol is flammable; wear eye protection.

Semi-quantitative results. Benedict's colour can be compared against standards of known glucose concentration to estimate the sugar content.

lessons.title: Heart, vessels and gas exchange
lessons.summary: The right ventricle pumps through the pulmonary artery to lungs; pulmonary veins return blood to the left side.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: The right ventricle pumps through the pulmonary artery to lungs; pulmonary veins return blood to the left side. The left ventricle pumps through the aorta to the body; venae cavae return blood. Coronary arteries supply heart muscle. Valves reduce backflow and a right-atrial pacemaker coordinates rate.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Arteries carry blood away under pressure and have muscular elastic walls. Veins return blood at lower pressure and have valves; thin capillaries permit exchange. Air travels through trachea and bronchi to alveoli, whose large area, thin walls and capillary supply support diffusion.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Double circulation. Blood passes through the heart twice in each circuit: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body. This keeps blood pressure high for the body circuit.

Heart rate and output. Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. For example, 75 cm³ × 70 beats/min = 5250 cm³/min (5.25 dm³/min). The natural pacemaker is a group of cells in the right atrium; artificial pacemakers correct irregular rhythms.

Vessels in exam answers. Arteries: thick muscular, elastic walls to withstand and smooth high pressure; narrow lumen. Veins: thinner walls, wide lumen, valves to stop backflow. Capillaries: one cell thick to allow diffusion. Rate of blood flow = volume ÷ time.

lessons.title: Blood and cardiovascular treatments
lessons.summary: Plasma transports dissolved materials including glucose, urea and carbon dioxide.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Plasma transports dissolved materials including glucose, urea and carbon dioxide. Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin and have a biconcave shape and no nucleus. White cells defend against pathogens; platelets help clot blood and reduce blood loss.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Fatty deposits narrow coronary arteries, reducing oxygen supply to heart muscle. Stents hold arteries open; statins reduce blood cholesterol. Replacement valves, pacemakers, donor hearts and temporary artificial hearts address different problems. Compare benefits with procedure risks, side effects and donor availability.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Red cell adaptations. No nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin; the biconcave shape gives a large surface area for oxygen diffusion; they are small and flexible to squeeze through capillaries. In the lungs haemoglobin combines with oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin, which releases oxygen in respiring tissues.

Treatments compared. Stents: quick, keep artery open, but risk of clotting near the stent. Statins: reduce LDL cholesterol, slow fatty deposits, but must be taken long-term and can have side effects. Valve replacement: mechanical valves last long but need anticoagulants; biological valves avoid that but wear out. Heart transplants need a donor and immunosuppressant drugs.

Fatty deposits narrow coronary arteries, reducing oxygen supply to heart muscle.

lessons.title: Health, risk factors and cancer
lessons.summary: Health includes physical and mental wellbeing.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Health includes physical and mental wellbeing. Communicable diseases spread between organisms; non-communicable ones do not. Risk factors increase probability, not certainty. Smoking increases lung disease risk; obesity increases type 2 diabetes risk; heavy alcohol use can damage liver tissue.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Correlation alone does not establish causation: age, diet or other confounders may explain an association. Cancer involves uncontrolled division. Benign tumours stay local; malignant tumours invade and can spread to form secondary tumours. Environmental exposure and inherited factors can both influence risk.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
How diseases interact. Defects in the immune system make infection more likely; some viruses can trigger cancers (for example HPV and cervical cancer); immune reactions to pathogens can trigger allergies; severe physical illness can lead to depression.

Lifestyle risk factors. Diet, smoking and lack of exercise affect cardiovascular disease; obesity is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes; alcohol affects the liver and brain; smoking and alcohol during pregnancy affect the unborn baby; carcinogens and ionising radiation increase cancer risk. The human and financial cost of non-communicable diseases is high for individuals, families and health services.

Reading data. Look for a correlation, then ask whether the sample was large, whether other factors were controlled, and whether a mechanism explains the link. Cancer risk factors include lifestyle and genetic factors.

lessons.summary: Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts; spongy mesophyll has air spaces.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts; spongy mesophyll has air spaces. Guard cells control stomata. Dead hollow lignified xylem carries water and mineral ions; living phloem translocates dissolved sugars from sources to tissues using or storing them.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Evaporation from leaf cells and diffusion through stomata drive transpiration. Replacement water moves up xylem from roots. Wind and warmth often increase loss; humidity reduces the water-vapour gradient. A potometer estimates water uptake, which differs slightly from transpiration because plants use some water.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Leaf tissues in order. Waxy cuticle and upper epidermis (transparent, reduces water loss) → palisade mesophyll (many chloroplasts for photosynthesis) → spongy mesophyll (air spaces for gas diffusion) → lower epidermis with stomata and guard cells. Xylem and phloem run in veins.

Guard cells. When guard cells take in water they become turgid and the stoma opens; when they lose water it closes, reducing water loss. More stomata are on the lower surface, which is cooler and shaded.

Potometer maths. Rate of water uptake = distance the bubble moves × cross-sectional area ÷ time. Area of the capillary = πr². Factors: light intensity (more stomata open), temperature, air movement and humidity.

lessons.title: Pathogens and named diseases
lessons.summary: Viruses reproduce inside host cells; bacteria can multiply and produce toxins.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Viruses reproduce inside host cells; bacteria can multiply and produce toxins. Measles spreads in droplets, causing fever and rash; HIV damages immune cells and can lead to AIDS. Tobacco mosaic virus causes discoloured leaf areas and reduces photosynthesis.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Salmonella causes food poisoning: hygiene and poultry vaccination reduce transmission. Gonorrhoea is bacterial and sexually transmitted. Rose black spot is fungal. Malaria is caused by a protist carried by mosquitoes: nets and removal of breeding sites reduce transmission.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Four types of pathogen. Viruses (measles, HIV, tobacco mosaic virus), bacteria (Salmonella, gonorrhoea), fungi (rose black spot), and protists (malaria). Pathogens spread by direct contact, by water, by air (droplets), or by vectors such as mosquitoes.

Controlling spread. Hygiene, destroying or controlling vectors, isolating infected individuals and vaccination all reduce transmission. Gonorrhoea is treated with antibiotics, though many strains are now resistant; condoms reduce its spread. HIV is controlled by antiretroviral drugs. lessons.title: Human defences and vaccination
lessons.summary: Skin forms a barrier and clots close wounds.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Skin forms a barrier and clots close wounds. Nose hairs and mucus trap particles; airway cilia move mucus towards the throat. Stomach acid kills many swallowed pathogens. White cells engulf pathogens, make specific antibodies and produce antitoxins.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Vaccines present harmless pathogen antigens and stimulate an immune response. Later exposure triggers faster specific antibody production, often preventing serious illness. High uptake reduces transmission and can protect vulnerable people. Compare rates in comparable populations rather than raw case totals.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Three ways white blood cells defend us. Phagocytosis: engulfing and digesting pathogens. Antibody production: lymphocytes make antibodies specific to the antigens on a pathogen, clumping it for destruction. Antitoxin production: antitoxins neutralise toxins released by bacteria.

Primary and secondary response. On first exposure antibody production is slow, so you may become ill. Memory cells remain. On a second exposure antibodies are produced much faster and in greater amounts, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms develop. A vaccine produces the first response without the illness.

Herd immunity. If a large proportion of a population is vaccinated, the pathogen cannot spread easily, protecting people who cannot be vaccinated.

lessons.title: Antibiotics and developing medicines
lessons.summary: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses reproducing inside cells.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses reproducing inside cells. Painkillers relieve symptoms without necessarily destroying pathogens. Penicillin came from mould; aspirin developed from willow chemistry and digitalis from foxgloves. Resistant strains make suitable prescribing important.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Preclinical tests use cells, tissues and animals. Low-dose healthy-volunteer trials examine safety before patient trials assess efficacy and dose. Random allocation and double-blind comparisons reduce bias; a placebo is useful where ethical. Sufficient sample size and peer review strengthen conclusions.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Antibiotic resistance. Mutations can make some bacteria resistant. When antibiotics are used, non-resistant bacteria die and resistant ones survive and reproduce, so the resistant strain spreads (for example MRSA). Reduce this by not prescribing antibiotics for viral or minor infections, finishing the full course, and limiting use in farming.

Drug development stages. Discovery → preclinical testing (cells, tissues, live animals) for toxicity and efficacy → clinical trial phase 1 (very low doses in healthy volunteers, for side effects) → phase 2 and 3 (patients, finding the optimum dose, compared with a placebo or existing drug) → peer review and publication → licensing.

Placebo and blinding. A placebo looks like the drug but has no active ingredient. In a double-blind trial neither patients nor doctors know who receives which, removing bias.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Monoclonal antibodies bind one particular antigen. Antibody-producing lymphocytes from an exposed mouse are fused with tumour cells to form hybridomas. A selected hybridoma is cloned and grown, combining antibody specificity with repeated division.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Pregnancy tests detect hCG using antibodies. Labelled antibodies locate molecules or disease markers; attached drugs can target cancer cells. Targeting may reduce healthy-tissue damage, but side effects, cost and uncertain effectiveness still matter.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Making them, in order. Inject a mouse with the chosen antigen → mouse lymphocytes make the specific antibody → remove lymphocytes and fuse with a tumour (myeloma) cell → hybridoma cell divides rapidly and makes the antibody → clone the hybridoma → collect and purify the antibodies.

Four uses. Pregnancy tests (antibodies bind hCG; a coloured line forms); measuring hormone or chemical levels and detecting pathogens in labs; locating specific molecules in cells or tissues using fluorescent dye; treating diseases such as cancer by carrying a radioactive substance, toxic drug or chemical that stops cell growth to cancer cells.

Evaluation. Monoclonal antibodies cause more side effects than first expected, are expensive to produce, and have not been as widely used as hoped.

lessons.title: Plant disease and defence
lessons.summary: Stunting, spots, decay and discolouration can indicate disease, but symptoms may have other causes.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Stunting, spots, decay and discolouration can indicate disease, but symptoms may have other causes. Manuals, laboratories and antibody-based tests aid diagnosis. Nitrate deficiency stunts growth through reduced protein synthesis; magnesium deficiency causes chlorosis through reduced chlorophyll. Aphids are pests rather than pathogens.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Cell walls, waxy cuticles and bark provide physical barriers. Plants may shed infected leaves or make antibacterial chemicals and poisons. Thorns and hairs deter herbivores. Link each defence to its threat; plants do not produce human white blood cells.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Identifying disease. Signs include stunted growth, spots on leaves, areas of decay, growths, malformed stems or leaves, discolouration and visible pests. Diagnosis uses a gardening manual or website, a lab test to identify the pathogen, or testing kits containing monoclonal antibodies.

Three groups of defence. Physical: cellulose cell walls, a tough waxy cuticle, and layers of dead cells (bark) that fall off. Chemical: antibacterial chemicals (such as mint and witch hazel oils) and poisons to deter herbivores. Mechanical: thorns and hairs, leaves that droop or curl when touched, and mimicry to trick animals.

Aphids feed on phloem sap and can spread viruses; ladybirds are a biological control.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and glucose uses
lessons.summary: Photosynthesis transfers light energy to chemical stores: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Photosynthesis transfers light energy to chemical stores: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. Chlorophyll absorbs light and the process is endothermic. Recognise CO₂, H₂O, C₆H₁₂O₆ and O₂. Plants respire continuously; photosynthesis needs light.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Glucose supplies respiration and can become starch, oils or cellulose. Nitrate ions supply nitrogen for amino acid and protein synthesis. Insoluble starch is useful for storage because it has little direct osmotic effect compared with an equivalent number of dissolved sugar molecules.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Balanced symbol equation. 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Light is needed, but it is not a reactant written in the equation. Energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts, so the reaction is endothermic.

Where the raw materials come from. Carbon dioxide diffuses in through stomata; water travels up the xylem from the roots; light is absorbed by chlorophyll in chloroplasts. Oxygen diffuses out of the leaf, or is used in respiration.

Five uses of glucose. Respiration; making starch for storage; making fats or oils for storage (seeds); making cellulose to strengthen cell walls; combining with nitrate ions to make amino acids and proteins.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Light, carbon dioxide, temperature and chlorophyll amount affect photosynthesis. At low light, increasing intensity often raises oxygen production. A horizontal curve shows constant rate rather than no photosynthesis; interpret what the axes actually measure.

lessons.summary: A limiting factor prevents further increase in photosynthesis under the current conditions.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: A limiting factor prevents further increase in photosynthesis under the current conditions. If extra carbon dioxide raises a plateau, carbon dioxide was limiting there. A different point may be limited by light or temperature; compare curves rather than assigning one universal limiting factor.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: In the point-source model, light intensity is proportional to 1/distance². Doubling distance quarters intensity. Greenhouse heating, lighting and carbon dioxide can increase yield only when useful; compare extra crop revenue against running costs to assess profit.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Inverse square law. Light intensity ∝ 1/d². Going from 10 cm to 30 cm makes intensity (10/30)² = 1/9 of the original. If intensity is 90 units at 10 cm, it is 10 units at 30 cm.

Interpreting limiting-factor graphs. On the rising part of a curve, the factor on the x-axis is limiting. Where the curve levels off, something else limits. If raising CO₂ gives a higher plateau, CO₂ was limiting at the plateau. Temperature affects enzymes; above the optimum the rate falls.

Greenhouses. Growers can add paraffin heaters (which also release CO₂), artificial lighting and CO₂ to maximise growth. A grower should only raise a factor while it is limiting and while the value of the extra crop is greater than the cost.

lessons.title: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration
lessons.summary: Respiration is an exothermic cellular process supplying energy for movement, synthesis and keeping warm.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Respiration is an exothermic cellular process supplying energy for movement, synthesis and keeping warm. Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water. Breathing moves air; it is not respiration. Both plants and animals respire.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Muscles respiring anaerobically form lactic acid and transfer less energy per glucose because breakdown is incomplete. Yeast and plant cells can produce ethanol and carbon dioxide anaerobically. Fermentation supplies carbon dioxide to raise bread dough and ethanol for alcoholic drinks.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Equations. Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, or C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Anaerobic in muscle: glucose → lactic acid. Anaerobic in plants and yeast (fermentation): glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.

Where and how much. Aerobic respiration happens mostly in mitochondria and transfers much more energy per glucose. Anaerobic respiration happens in the cytoplasm because glucose is only partly broken down.

Uses of energy. Chemical reactions to build larger molecules, muscle contraction for movement, and keeping warm. Respiration happens continuously in all living cells.

lessons.title: Exercise responses and metabolism
lessons.summary: Exercise raises muscular energy demand.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Exercise raises muscular energy demand. Heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase, supplying oxygen and glucose and removing carbon dioxide. Insufficient oxygen leads to additional anaerobic respiration and lactic acid accumulation, contributing to fatigue.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Metabolism is all reactions in cells or an organism: respiration, making carbohydrates from glucose, lipids from glycerol and fatty acids, and proteins from amino acids. Excess amino acids are broken down to form urea. Plants need nitrate ions when synthesising amino acids.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Investigating exercise. Measure resting pulse and breathing rate, then exercise for a set time (for example 3 minutes of step-ups) and measure every minute during recovery. Repeat with several people. Control the type and intensity of exercise. Recovery time is a measure of fitness.

Why rates rise. Muscles respire faster, needing more oxygen and glucose and producing more CO₂. Increased heart rate delivers more oxygenated blood; deeper, faster breathing increases gas exchange in the alveoli.

Metabolism, Higher detail. The liver converts lactic acid back into glucose and breaks down excess amino acids (deamination) to form urea, which the kidneys excrete.

keypoints: Exercise raises muscular energy demand.
Metabolism is all reactions in cells or an organism: respiration, making carbohydrates from glucose, lipids from glycerol and fatty acids, and proteins from amino acids.

lessons.title: Lactic acid and oxygen debt
lessons.summary: After intense exercise, blood carries lactic acid from muscles to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: After intense exercise, blood carries lactic acid from muscles to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose. The extra oxygen needed during recovery to remove accumulated lactic acid is called oxygen debt in the GCSE model.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: An oxygen-uptake trace returns gradually towards resting levels. Compare recovery uptake with the resting baseline rather than counting all oxygen breathed. An extra 1.5 litres each minute over four minutes totals six litres in a simplified constant-rate example.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Muscle fatigue. During long periods of vigorous activity, muscles become fatigued and stop contracting efficiently. Anaerobic respiration supplies extra energy but makes lactic acid, which builds up.

Repaying the debt. After exercise, breathing stays fast and deep and heart rate stays high. Blood carries lactic acid to the liver, which converts it to glucose; this needs oxygen. Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from cells.

From a graph. Extra oxygen = (recovery uptake − resting uptake) × time, or the area between the recovery curve and the resting line.

lessons.title: Homeostasis, neurones and reflexes
lessons.summary: Homeostasis maintains suitable internal conditions for cells, including temperature, glucose and water levels.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Homeostasis maintains suitable internal conditions for cells, including temperature, glucose and water levels. Receptors detect stimuli, coordination centres process information and effectors respond. The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; electrical impulses travel along neurones.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: A reflex pathway includes receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone and effector. Chemical transmitters cross synapses. Reflexes are rapid and automatic without conscious decision-making, protecting against damage. The brain can receive information without initiating the first protective response.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
The synapse in detail. When an impulse reaches the end of a neurone, a chemical neurotransmitter is released. It diffuses across the tiny gap (synapse) and binds to receptors on the next neurone, starting a new electrical impulse. Synapses slow transmission slightly and make sure impulses travel one way.

Control system pattern. stimulus → receptor → coordinator (brain, spinal cord or pancreas) → effector (muscle contracts or gland secretes) → response. Homeostasis uses both nervous and hormonal responses.

Speed calculations. Speed = distance ÷ time. An impulse travelling 1.2 m in 0.012 s moves at 100 m/s.

keypoints: Homeostasis maintains suitable internal conditions for cells, including temperature, glucose and water levels.
A reflex pathway includes receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone and effector.

lessons.title: Investigating reaction time
lessons.summary: A falling ruler caught by a participant provides a distance used to estimate reaction time through a conversion table.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: A falling ruler caught by a participant provides a distance used to estimate reaction time through a conversion table. Investigate a safe factor such as distraction or practice. Obtain consent, permit withdrawal and do not administer medication or deprive participants of sleep.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Keep the start position, catching hand and release procedure constant. Randomise condition order to reduce practice effects; repeat across participants. Distance is not time, so report units honestly and use a suitable conversion before quoting seconds.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Converting distance to time. The ruler falls from rest with acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s², so t = √(2d ÷ g). A catch at 20 cm gives t = √(2 × 0.20 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 0.20 s. Many textbooks give a conversion table instead.

Designing a fair test. Independent variable: the factor being tested (for example caffeine-free drink vs. none, music vs. silence, dominant vs. non-dominant hand). Dependent: catch distance. Controls: same ruler, same starting position with zero at the thumb, same person dropping without warning, same number of practice trials.

Ethics. Participants give informed consent, can withdraw and are not given drugs. Data should be anonymised.

lessons.title: Brain regions and their roles
lessons.summary: The cerebral cortex supports conscious thought, memory and language.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: The cerebral cortex supports conscious thought, memory and language. The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance; the medulla controls automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate. Regions are highly interconnected rather than isolated units.

notes.title: Identify regions on a diagram
notes.html: Locate the large folded cerebral cortex, the smaller cerebellum towards the back, and the medulla in the brainstem. Associate each region with its main functions. A labelled diagram is a model of a complex organ; use landmarks and relative positions rather than relying only on colours.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Why the brain is hard to study. It contains billions of interconnected neurones; functions spread across several regions; it is protected by the skull; and damage can be permanent. This limits how we can treat brain damage or disease.

Other regions you may meet. The hypothalamus (temperature, water balance) and the pituitary gland lie under the brain. In exams, stick to the three AQA regions unless the question introduces more.

Answering label questions. Cerebral cortex: the large, wrinkled outer layer (consciousness, intelligence, memory, language). Cerebellum: the small, ridged region at the back underneath (muscular coordination and balance). Medulla: joins the brain to the spinal cord (unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing).

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Brain mapping uses observations of patients with damage, electrical stimulation and MRI. Each provides different evidence: scans show structures and patient observations link damage to function. Electrical stimulation can reveal a response when a region is activated.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Complex connections make cause and effect difficult to isolate. Brain tissue is delicate and procedures can cause irreversible harm. Evaluate consent, likely clinical benefit, uncertainties and risks; a clear observed response does not justify every invasive investigation.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Three methods compared. Studying patients with brain damage: links damage in one area to lost function, but damage is uncontrolled and may affect several regions. Electrical stimulation: electrodes stimulate a region during surgery and the response (movement, memory) is recorded; precise, but invasive. MRI scans: show which regions are active (fMRI) or their structure; non-invasive, but expensive and show correlation rather than cause.

Ethical points. Patients must consent; invasive methods should only be used when there is a clinical benefit; data must be kept confidential.

lessons.title: The eye and accommodation
lessons.summary: Cornea and lens refract light onto the retina; the optic nerve carries impulses.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Cornea and lens refract light onto the retina; the optic nerve carries impulses. The sclera protects the eye. The iris changes pupil size: circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax in bright light, reducing entry; dim light reverses this.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: For near focus, ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens becomes thicker. For distance, muscles relax, ligaments tighten and the lens thins. Myopia focuses before the retina and uses a concave correcting lens; hyperopia focuses behind and uses a convex lens. Treatments have benefits and risks.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Structures and functions. Retina: light receptors (rods and cones). Optic nerve: carries impulses to the brain. Sclera: tough white outer layer. Cornea: transparent front that refracts light. Iris: muscles control pupil size. Ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments: change lens shape.

Treatments. Glasses or contact lenses; laser surgery to reshape the cornea; replacement lens surgery. Laser surgery may remove the need for glasses but carries risks such as infection or worsened vision.

Iris reflex. In bright light, circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax, so the pupil gets smaller. This protects the retina from damage.

lessons.title: Body temperature control
lessons.summary: The thermoregulatory centre in the brain monitors blood temperature and receives input from skin receptors.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: The thermoregulatory centre in the brain monitors blood temperature and receives input from skin receptors. Too much warmth triggers sweating and dilation of vessels supplying skin. Cold triggers less sweating, constriction of skin vessels and shivering.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Begin an answer with the direction of the temperature change, then identify the response. Do not claim capillaries move nearer the skin. Distinguish the controlled internal temperature from changing outside temperature; these are automatic control responses, not conscious decisions.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Normal core temperature. About 37 °C, the optimum for many human enzymes. Temperature receptors in the thermoregulatory centre (hypothalamus) detect blood temperature; receptors in the skin detect external changes.

Responses summary. Too hot: sweat glands release more sweat; blood vessels supplying skin capillaries dilate (vasodilation). Too cold: less sweating; skin vessels constrict (vasoconstriction); skeletal muscles contract rapidly (shivering) and hairs stand up.

Why it matters. If core temperature rises too high enzymes start to denature; if it falls too low reactions become too slow.

Begin an answer with the direction of the temperature change, then identify the response.

lessons.title: Explaining thermoregulation
lessons.summary: Evaporation of sweat transfers energy from skin to the surroundings.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Evaporation of sweat transfers energy from skin to the surroundings. Vasodilation increases blood flow near the surface and energy transfer. In humid air, reduced evaporation can make sweating less effective, so visible sweat does not guarantee efficient cooling.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Vasoconstriction reduces surface blood flow and energy loss. Shivering involves muscle contraction and increased respiration, transferring energy to thermal stores. These responses oppose a fall in temperature and reduce when conditions recover: negative feedback.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Energy transfer explanations. Vasodilation: more blood flows through skin capillaries, so more energy is transferred to the surroundings by radiation. Sweating: water evaporates using energy from the skin. Vasoconstriction: less blood near the surface, so less energy is lost. Shivering: muscle contraction needs respiration, which transfers energy to heat the body.

Negative feedback. Any change away from the set point triggers responses that reverse it; once temperature returns to normal, the response stops. This keeps temperature within narrow limits.

Common error. Blood vessels do not move closer to or further from the skin; it is the volume of blood flowing through skin capillaries that changes.

Vasoconstriction reduces surface blood flow and energy loss.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.

lessons.title: Endocrine glands, insulin and diabetes
lessons.summary: Endocrine glands release hormones into blood; target tissues respond.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Endocrine glands release hormones into blood; target tissues respond. Effects are often slower and longer-lasting than nervous responses. Know pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, pancreas, ovaries and testes. Pituitary hormones influence several other glands.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: High glucose stimulates pancreatic insulin, increasing glucose uptake and conversion to glycogen in liver and muscle. Type 1 diabetes involves too little insulin; type 2 involves poor cellular response to insulin. Insulin treatment, diet, exercise and other medicines have different roles depending on the condition.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Glands and hormones. Pituitary (master gland: FSH, LH, ADH, TSH, growth hormone); thyroid (thyroxine); adrenal glands (adrenaline); pancreas (insulin, glucagon); ovaries (oestrogen, progesterone); testes (testosterone).

Comparing type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Type 1: the pancreas produces little or no insulin; usually starts in childhood; treated with insulin injections. Type 2: body cells no longer respond to insulin; strongly linked to obesity; treated with a carbohydrate-controlled diet and exercise, sometimes drugs.

Reading glucose graphs. After a glucose drink, blood glucose rises then falls within about two hours in a healthy person. In someone with diabetes it rises higher and stays high for longer.

keypoints: Endocrine glands release hormones into blood; target tissues respond.
High glucose stimulates pancreatic insulin, increasing glucose uptake and conversion to glycogen in liver and muscle.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

lessons.title: Glucagon, adrenaline and thyroxine
lessons.summary: Low glucose stimulates pancreatic glucagon, causing liver glycogen to become glucose released into blood.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Low glucose stimulates pancreatic glucagon, causing liver glycogen to become glucose released into blood. Insulin and glucagon oppose departures from normal glucose levels. Corrective secretion decreases as conditions recover: negative feedback does not mean every response always lowers every variable.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Adrenaline from adrenals increases heart rate and oxygen/glucose delivery for fight or flight. Thyroxine from thyroid regulates basal metabolic rate and development. Low thyroxine stimulates pituitary signals promoting secretion; high thyroxine inhibits those signals.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Insulin and glucagon working together. High blood glucose → pancreas secretes insulin → glucose enters cells; liver and muscles store glycogen → glucose falls. Low blood glucose → pancreas secretes glucagon → liver converts glycogen to glucose → glucose rises. Remember: glycogen is the storage carbohydrate; glucagon is the hormone.

Adrenaline. Released in times of fear or stress. It increases heart rate and boosts oxygen and glucose delivery to the brain and muscles, preparing the body for fight or flight. This is not negative feedback.

Thyroxine. Stimulates basal metabolic rate and is important for growth and development. Its level is controlled by negative feedback via TSH from the pituitary.

keypoints: Low glucose stimulates pancreatic glucagon, causing liver glycogen to become glucose released into blood.
Adrenaline from adrenals increases heart rate and oxygen/glucose delivery for fight or flight.

lessons.title: Kidneys, excretion and treatment
lessons.summary: Kidneys remove urea and regulate water and ions.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Excess amino acids are broken down and form urea in the liver; blood carries urea to kidneys for excretion. Kidneys regulate water and ions. Carbon dioxide leaves through lungs; water, ions and a little urea also leave in sweat. Cells losing or gaining too much water by osmosis do not work efficiently.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Dialysis removes waste through a partially permeable membrane using carefully balanced dialysis fluid. It requires regular treatment. A transplant can restore continuous function but requires a donor, surgery and management of rejection. Do not confuse producing urea in the liver with removing it in kidneys.

notes.title: Filtration and reabsorption
notes.html: Kidneys filter blood and selectively reabsorb useful substances such as glucose, some ions and water. Urine normally contains urea, excess ions and water rather than blood cells. Compare values before and after filtration using the units and volumes given; the structure of the nephron is beyond this GCSE requirement.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Water balance. Water leaves the body via the lungs in exhaled air, via the skin in sweat, and via the kidneys in urine. Ions are lost in sweat and urine. Only urine loss is controlled.

Dialysis in detail. Blood flows next to dialysis fluid, separated by a partially permeable membrane. The fluid contains the same concentration of glucose and useful ions as normal blood, so these do not diffuse out, but no urea, so urea diffuses out. Excess ions and water also leave. Sessions last several hours, several times a week.

Transplants. A donor kidney must have a similar tissue type; immunosuppressant drugs stop rejection but increase infection risk. Transplants are cheaper long-term than dialysis but there are too few donors.

keypoints: Urea is produced in the liver and removed from blood by the kidneys.
Dialysis removes waste through a partially permeable membrane using carefully balanced dialysis fluid.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

lessons.title: Selective reabsorption and ADH
lessons.summary: Kidneys filter blood and selectively reabsorb all glucose, appropriate ions and sufficient water.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Kidneys filter blood and selectively reabsorb all glucose, appropriate ions and sufficient water. Amino-acid deamination removes the nitrogen-containing part in the liver; ammonia is converted to urea for safer excretion. These details explain why urine composition differs from blood.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Low blood water level is detected in the brain; pituitary ADH increases kidney-tubule permeability, so more water returns to blood. Urine becomes smaller in volume and more concentrated. Plenty of water reduces ADH and increases dilute urine. ADH changes reabsorption, not water creation.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Deamination. Excess amino acids cannot be stored. In the liver the amine group is removed to form ammonia, which is toxic, so it is immediately converted to urea for safe excretion.

Negative feedback with ADH. Blood too concentrated → detected by brain receptors → pituitary releases more ADH → kidney tubules more permeable → more water reabsorbed → small volume of concentrated urine → blood concentration returns to normal → ADH release falls. Blood too dilute → less ADH → less water reabsorbed → large volume of dilute urine.

Data questions. Glucose is present in blood and filtrate but normally absent in urine because it is all reabsorbed. Urea concentration rises in urine because water is reabsorbed.

keypoints: Kidneys filter blood and selectively reabsorb all glucose, appropriate ions and sufficient water.
Low blood water level is detected in the brain; pituitary ADH increases kidney-tubule permeability, so more water returns to blood.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.why: ADH makes tubules more permeable to water.
