ms: The brain detects low blood water concentration and the pituitary releases more ADH.
Kidney tubules become more permeable and reabsorb more water.
A smaller volume of more concentrated urine is produced.

exam.q: Explain why glucose is found in the filtrate but not in the urine of a healthy person.
ms: Glucose is small enough to be filtered out of blood.
All glucose is selectively reabsorbed back into blood.

Pituitary releases more ADH into the blood.

lessons.title: Reproductive hormones and contraception
lessons.summary: Testosterone from testes supports sperm production and male secondary sexual characteristics; ovarian oestrogen supports female development.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Testosterone from testes supports sperm production and male secondary sexual characteristics; ovarian oestrogen supports female development. FSH matures an egg and LH triggers ovulation. Oestrogen and progesterone maintain the uterus lining. Twenty-eight days is a cycle model; real cycle lengths vary.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Hormonal methods can inhibit egg maturation or release. Barriers prevent sperm reaching eggs; condoms also reduce some STI transmission. Intrauterine devices, spermicides, fertility-awareness methods and sterilisation differ in effectiveness, risks and reversibility. Compare typical-use data where given.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Four hormones in the menstrual cycle. FSH (pituitary): causes an egg to mature in the ovary. LH (pituitary): stimulates release of the egg (ovulation). Oestrogen (ovaries): causes the uterus lining to grow. Progesterone (ovaries): maintains the uterus lining.

Puberty. Reproductive hormones cause secondary sex characteristics. Oestrogen is the main female hormone; testosterone, made in the testes, stimulates sperm production.

Contraception summary. Hormonal: oral pill (oestrogen and progesterone inhibit FSH), injection, implant or skin patch (slow-release progesterone). Non-hormonal: condoms and diaphragms (barriers), IUDs, spermicidal agents, abstaining around ovulation, and sterilisation.

Hormonal methods can inhibit egg maturation or release.

Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

lessons.title: Hormone interactions and IVF
lessons.summary: FSH stimulates egg maturation and oestrogen secretion.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: FSH stimulates egg maturation and oestrogen secretion. Oestrogen rebuilds the lining, inhibits FSH and stimulates an LH surge. LH causes ovulation; progesterone maintains the lining and inhibits FSH/LH. Falling progesterone allows the lining to break down if pregnancy does not occur.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Fertility drugs use FSH/LH. IVF matures several eggs, collects them, fertilises them in a laboratory and transfers one or two early embryos to the uterus. Success is uncertain; consider physical and emotional demands, cost and multiple-pregnancy risks as well as benefits.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Hormone interactions over the cycle. Days 1–5: menstruation. FSH rises → egg matures and ovary releases oestrogen. Oestrogen rises → lining thickens, FSH is inhibited, LH surge is stimulated. Around day 14: LH surge → ovulation. Progesterone from the empty follicle (corpus luteum) maintains the lining and inhibits FSH and LH. If no pregnancy, progesterone falls and menstruation begins.

Treating infertility. FSH and LH in a fertility drug can help a woman release eggs. IVF: FSH and LH stimulate several eggs to mature; eggs collected and fertilised with sperm in the lab; fertilised eggs develop into embryos; one or two embryos inserted into the uterus.

Issues. Emotional and physical stress, low success rates (about 25–30% per cycle) and multiple births, which are riskier for mother and babies. Some people object to unused embryos being destroyed.

Fertility drugs use FSH/LH.

lessons.title: Plant growth responses
lessons.summary: Shoots grow towards light and against gravity; roots usually grow with gravity.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Shoots grow towards light and against gravity; roots usually grow with gravity. These are directional growth responses, not movement of the whole plant. Auxin is associated with unequal growth. Label phototropism and gravitropism using the stimulus and response direction.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Test similar seedlings with one-sided light and a suitable control, or change orientation while controlling illumination. Keep age, species, water and temperature constant. Repeat and record lengths and labelled drawings. Change light or gravity separately to isolate the factor.

notes.title: Unequal growth
notes.html: Plant hormones coordinate growth. Unequal auxin distribution causes different growth rates on opposite sides of a root or shoot, producing bending. This is growth through differential elongation rather than a muscle contraction.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Required practical: seedlings. Germinate cress or mustard seeds on damp cotton wool in Petri dishes. Shine light from one side (inside a box with a slot) and use a dish in uniform light or darkness as a control. Measure shoot length and angle of curvature each day with a protractor. For gravitropism, pin seedlings at different orientations in a clinostat or turn the dish.

Variables. Independent: direction of light (or orientation). Dependent: direction and amount of growth. Control: same species, number of seeds, volume of water, temperature.

Why it matters. Shoots growing towards light can photosynthesise more; roots growing down anchor the plant and reach water and minerals.

lessons.title: Explaining and using plant hormones
lessons.summary: In a shoot lit from one side, auxin accumulates on the shaded side and promotes elongation, causing bending towards light.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: In a shoot lit from one side, auxin accumulates on the shaded side and promotes elongation, causing bending towards light. Auxin inhibits elongation in roots at concentrations that promote shoot growth, helping explain opposite responses to gravity.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Auxins are used in rooting powders, tissue culture and selective weedkillers. Gibberellins promote germination, flowering and fruit growth. Ethene controls ripening, allowing timing after transport. Link hormone action to benefit and consider dose, cost and non-target effects.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Gravitropism explained. In a horizontal root, auxin collects on the lower side. In roots, auxin inhibits growth, so the upper side grows faster and the root bends down. In a horizontal shoot, auxin collects on the lower side and stimulates growth, so the shoot bends up.

Uses in agriculture. Auxins: weedkillers that affect broad-leaved weeds but not grasses or cereals; rooting powders; tissue culture. Ethene: controls ripening during storage and transport. Gibberellins: end seed dormancy, promote flowering, increase fruit size.

Evaluating use. Benefits include higher yields and less waste; concerns include effects on non-target species and residues.

lessons.title: Reproduction, meiosis and fertilisation
lessons.summary: Sexual reproduction joins gametes and mixes genetic information.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Sexual reproduction joins gametes and mixes genetic information. DNA is replicated once before meiosis, followed by two cell divisions, making four genetically different cells with half the original chromosome number. Examples. Gametes in animals are sperm and eggs; in flowering plants they are pollen and egg cells.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Asexual reproduction is fast, needs no mate and preserves a successful genotype in favourable conditions. Sexual reproduction requires more time and energy but generates variation, improving the chance that some offspring survive a changed environment or new disease.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: DNA is a polymer with two strands forming a double helix. Chromosomes contain DNA; genes are sections coding for amino acid sequences in proteins. A genome is the entire genetic material of an organism. Alleles are versions of genes, not additional organelles.

lessons.title: DNA nucleotides and triplets

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: A DNA nucleotide contains sugar, phosphate and one base: A, C, G or T. Repeated sugar and phosphate groups form the backbone. Groups of three bases code for amino acids, so base order determines the order of amino acids.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Proteins are amino acid chains, not DNA-base chains. A simplified coding sequence of twelve bases has four triplets. This calculation is a model rather than a claim that real genes contain only uninterrupted coding DNA.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Complementary strands. In a DNA molecule, A always pairs with T and C with G on the opposite strand. If one strand reads ATG GCA, the other reads TAC CGT. Equal numbers: if 20% of bases are A, 20% are T, leaving 60% shared equally by C and G (30% each).

Triplet code. Each sequence of three bases codes for one amino acid; the order of triplets determines the order of amino acids, which determines the protein's shape and function.

Non-coding DNA. Not all DNA codes for protein; some parts switch genes on and off.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Complementary bases pair A–T and C–G. A template carries gene instructions to ribosomes; carrier molecules bring amino acids in sequence. The completed chain folds into a functional shape. Detailed RNA structures are beyond the GCSE requirement.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Many mutations have little effect, but some alter amino acids, folding and protein function. Non-coding variants can change gene expression instead of protein sequence. Explain the intermediate protein effect before predicting a phenotype; not every mutation is harmful.

lessons.title: Alleles, disorders and sex inheritance
lessons.summary: Genotype describes alleles and phenotype describes expressed characteristics.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Genotype describes alleles and phenotype describes expressed characteristics. Homozygous means identical alleles; heterozygous means different alleles. A dominant allele is expressed in a heterozygote. Dominant does not mean more common, stronger or beneficial.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Cystic fibrosis uses a recessive inheritance model; polydactyly can be dominant. Interpret pedigrees using the stated symbols and model. In the standard sex-chromosome model, XX is female and XY male; sperm can supply X or Y, giving approximately equal probabilities.

notes.title: Evaluate embryo screening
notes.html: Genetic screening can identify embryos carrying a disorder allele before implantation. Potential benefits include reducing the chance of a serious inherited condition, while limitations include cost, uncertain predictions and ethical concerns about selecting embryos. notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Key words. Gamete, chromosome, gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype, phenotype. Most characteristics are controlled by several genes working together; single-gene examples are useful models.

Embryo screening issues. It is expensive; some people think it implies disabled people are less valued; there are fears of 'designer babies'. Supporters argue it reduces suffering. Embryo screening is regulated by law in the UK.

lessons.title: Variation, natural selection and selective breeding
lessons.summary: Variation can be genetic, environmental or both.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Variation can be genetic, environmental or both. Mutations create new variants and sexual reproduction reshuffles information. Inherited variants improving survival and reproduction can become more frequent over generations through natural selection. Individuals do not deliberately evolve because they need to.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Selective breeding chooses parents with desired traits, breeds them, selects suitable offspring and repeats. It can improve yield but reduce genetic diversity and increase inherited defects through inbreeding. Distinguish human choice of parents from environmental selection.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Natural selection step by step. (1) Variation exists due to mutations. (2) More offspring are produced than can survive; there is competition. (3) Individuals with characteristics best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and breed. (4) They pass on their alleles. (5) Over many generations the advantageous allele becomes more common. If two populations become so different they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, a new species has formed.

Selective breeding examples. Disease-resistant crops, cows with high milk yield, dogs with a gentle nature, large or unusual flowers. Inbreeding increases the chance of harmful recessive alleles pairing, so some breeds are prone to disease.

lessons.title: Cloning plants and animals
lessons.summary: Cuttings and sterile tissue culture reproduce useful plant genotypes.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Cuttings and sterile tissue culture reproduce useful plant genotypes. They can rapidly produce many plants, but low diversity creates shared vulnerability. Embryo transplants split early unspecialised embryo cells before implantation into host mothers.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Adult-cell cloning replaces an egg nucleus with an adult body-cell nucleus, stimulates development and implants the embryo. Nuclear DNA matches the body-cell donor. Consider low success, animal welfare and conservation potential rather than describing cloning as risk-free.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Four methods. Tissue culture: small groups of plant cells grown on nutrient medium to make clones (for rare plants and commercial nurseries). Cuttings: gardeners take cuttings to grow identical plants quickly. Embryo transplants: cells split from an early embryo before specialisation; identical embryos implanted in host mothers. Adult cell cloning: nucleus removed from an unfertilised egg; nucleus from an adult body cell inserted; electric shock stimulates division; embryo implanted (Dolly the sheep, 1996).

Issues. Low genetic variety; possible health problems in cloned animals; ethical concerns about using the method for humans; benefits for conserving endangered species.

lessons.title: Darwin, Wallace, Mendel and speciation
lessons.summary: Darwin and Wallace independently developed natural selection.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Darwin and Wallace independently developed natural selection. Acceptance was slowed by limited evidence, religious beliefs and poor understanding of inheritance. Lamarck proposed inherited acquired characteristics, which does not generally explain genetic evolution. Mendel found inheritance patterns through pea crosses before DNA was understood.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Isolation prevents gene flow between populations. Different conditions favour different alleles and mutations add variation. Over generations, populations may diverge until they cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring. New genetic evidence can revise scientific explanations.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Evidence Darwin used. Observations on the Galápagos (finches with different beaks on different islands), knowledge from selective breeding, and fossils. He published On the Origin of Species in 1859.

Why acceptance was slow. The theory challenged the idea that God made all animals and plants; there was not enough evidence at the time; the mechanism of inheritance and variation was unknown until 50 years later.

Wallace worked on warning colouration and speciation. Mendel found that characteristics are determined by 'units' passed on unchanged; his work was recognised only after his death, when chromosomes and later DNA were discovered.

lessons.title: Fossils, extinction and resistance
lessons.summary: Fossils form from preserved remains, mineral replacement or traces such as footprints.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Fossils form from preserved remains, mineral replacement or traces such as footprints. The record is incomplete because soft organisms decay, fossilisation is unusual and rocks can be destroyed. Extinction can follow habitat change, new predators, disease or catastrophic events.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Random variants can give antibiotic resistance. Antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant survivors to reproduce. Treatment selects existing variants rather than making bacteria choose to adapt. Appropriate prescribing and infection prevention help reduce selection and transmission.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
How fossils form. (1) Parts of organisms that have not decayed because conditions (lack of oxygen, moisture or the right temperature) prevented decay. (2) Hard parts replaced by minerals as they decay. (3) Preserved traces such as footprints, burrows and root pathways.

What fossils show. How much or how little organisms have changed over time. Early forms of life were soft-bodied, so they left few traces.

MRSA. Resistant bacteria are not killed, so they spread. To reduce the rate of resistance: doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately; patients complete the course; agricultural use is restricted. New antibiotics are slow and expensive to develop.

lessons.title: Classification and evolutionary trees
lessons.summary: The hierarchy is kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: The hierarchy is kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Binomial names combine genus and species. Trees represent proposed common ancestry; organisms sharing a more recent common ancestor are more closely related.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Molecular and improved microscopic evidence led to Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryota as domains. Similar appearance need not imply close relationship. Read a tree through its branching points rather than the physical distance between printed names.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Linnaeus's system. Organisms were classified by structure and characteristics into kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Binomial names (for example Homo sapiens) use genus then species, written in italics with a capital letter for the genus only.

Three-domain system. Carl Woese, using chemical analysis, proposed Archaea (primitive bacteria often in extreme environments), Bacteria (true bacteria) and Eukaryota (protists, fungi, plants and animals).

Evolutionary trees use current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct ones to show how closely related organisms are.

lessons.title: Communities and environmental factors
lessons.summary: A population is one species in an area; a community includes all populations; an ecosystem includes the non-living environment.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: A population is one species in an area; a community includes all populations; an ecosystem includes the non-living environment. Plants compete for light, water, minerals and space; animals for food, mates and territory. Interdependence links species through feeding, pollination and shelter.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Biotic factors include predators, pathogens and competitors. Abiotic factors include temperature, light, oxygen, water and pH. Changing one factor may affect many populations. Stability means relatively balanced populations, not numbers that never vary.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Levels of organisation. Individual → population → community → ecosystem. A habitat is the place where an organism lives.

Interdependence in action. In a woodland, trees provide food and shelter; insects pollinate flowers; birds disperse seeds; decomposers recycle nutrients. Removing one species, such as bees, can reduce plant reproduction and affect animals that eat fruits and seeds.

Abiotic and biotic factors to name. Abiotic: light intensity, temperature, moisture, soil pH and mineral content, wind intensity and direction, CO₂ for plants, O₂ for aquatic animals. Biotic: availability of food, new predators, new pathogens, one species outcompeting another.

lessons.title: Adaptations and extremophiles
lessons.summary: Adaptations can be structural, behavioural or functional.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Adaptations can be structural, behavioural or functional. Link a feature to its environmental challenge and survival benefit. Thick insulation conserves thermal energy; nocturnal activity can avoid daytime heat. Individuals do not acquire inherited adaptations simply because they need them.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Extremophiles inhabit conditions such as high heat, pressure or salinity. Desert plants may have waxy cuticles, reduced leaves and water stores. Trade-offs matter: reducing leaf area conserves water but can reduce light capture. Different adaptations may solve the same problem.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Three types of adaptation. Structural: features of body shape or structure, such as thick fur, small ears in the Arctic fox, or spines in cacti. Behavioural: actions such as migration, hibernation or burrowing. Functional: processes such as producing concentrated urine, or reproduction timed to food supply.

Surface area to volume and heat. Large animals with small ears and compact bodies have a small SA:V and lose less heat (polar bear). Desert animals like the fennec fox have large ears to radiate heat.

Extremophiles. Bacteria in hot vents, deep-sea organisms at high pressure, and organisms in very salty lakes have enzymes and membranes suited to these conditions.

lessons.title: Food chains and predator–prey cycles
lessons.summary: Producers make biomass, usually by photosynthesis.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Producers make biomass, usually by photosynthesis. Primary consumers eat producers and secondary consumers eat primary consumers. Arrows show biomass movement from food to feeder. Food webs represent several linked feeding relationships.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: More prey can support predator reproduction; more predators can reduce prey, after which predators may decline through food shortage. Changes lag rather than occurring instantly. Weather, disease and competition also influence real populations, so simple cycles are models.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Trophic language. Producer → primary consumer (herbivore) → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer. Apex predators are carnivores with no predators. Decomposers break down dead material.

Predator–prey graphs. The prey peak comes first; the predator peak follows because predators need time to breed. Predator numbers are usually lower than prey numbers.

Food web reasoning. When one population changes, follow every arrow into and out of it. A fall in rabbits might mean foxes eat more voles, so voles fall as well.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Use random coordinates to avoid choosing favourable quadrat locations. Count consistently and repeat widely. Mean count divided by quadrat area gives density; density times habitat area estimates population. Uneven distribution makes this an estimate, not an exact census.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: A transect investigates distribution along a gradient. Use quadrats at measured intervals and measure the relevant abiotic factor. Repeat transects and standardise counting rules. A correlation with light does not rule out variation in moisture or soil.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Required practical: random sampling. Lay two tape measures at right angles to make a grid. Use random number tables or a calculator to generate coordinates. Place a quadrat at each coordinate and count the species. Repeat for at least 10 quadrats.

Population estimate. Population = (total area ÷ quadrat area) × mean number per quadrat. Example: mean 4 daisies per 0.25 m² quadrat in a 2000 m² field gives (2000 ÷ 0.25) × 4 = 32 000.

Transects. Lay a tape from one habitat to another (for example shade to open field), place quadrats at regular intervals and record species and an abiotic factor (light meter, soil moisture). Abundance can be recorded as count or percentage cover.

lessons.title: Carbon and water cycles
lessons.summary: Photosynthesis incorporates atmospheric carbon into biomass; feeding passes it between organisms.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Photosynthesis incorporates atmospheric carbon into biomass; feeding passes it between organisms. Respiration by plants, animals and decomposers returns carbon dioxide. Decomposition returns mineral ions to soil; combustion releases stored carbon dioxide. Matter is recycled rather than created.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Evaporation and transpiration transfer water to air, condensation forms clouds and precipitation returns it. Runoff and soil movement return water to rivers and oceans. Materials cycle, whereas energy eventually dissipates to surroundings and is not recycled in the same way.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Carbon cycle processes. Photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration by plants, animals and microorganisms returns CO₂; feeding passes carbon compounds along food chains; death and decay pass carbon to decomposers; combustion of wood and fossil fuels releases CO₂. Fossil fuels formed from organisms that did not decay.

Water cycle. Evaporation from seas, transpiration from plants, condensation into clouds, precipitation, and runoff or percolation through soil. Water is used by plants for photosynthesis and support (turgor) and by animals for many processes.

Why decomposers matter. They return carbon to the atmosphere and mineral ions to the soil, which plants then absorb.

lessons.summary: Biodiversity is the variety of species.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Biodiversity is the variety of species. It supports stable food webs and resources such as food and potential medicines. Human population growth and consumption increase waste, including sewage, fertilisers, toxic chemicals, smoke and acidic gases.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Farming, building, quarrying and waste disposal can destroy habitats. Deforestation reduces habitats and releases carbon through burning or decay. Peat stores partly decomposed carbon; draining or extracting it damages habitats and releases carbon dioxide. Explain both ecological effects and the demands driving land use.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Pollution types. Water: sewage, fertiliser runoff and toxic chemicals. Land: landfill and toxic chemicals. Air: smoke and acidic gases (sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides) causing acid rain.

Eutrophication. Fertiliser runoff → algae grow rapidly → algae block light → plants below die → decomposers feed on dead plants and use up oxygen → fish die.

Deforestation. Large-scale clearing in tropical areas for cattle, rice and biofuel crops reduces biodiversity, increases CO₂ (less photosynthesis, burning and decay) and removes carbon stores.

Peat. Peat bogs store carbon; draining them for agriculture or extracting peat for compost releases CO₂ and destroys habitats. Gardeners can choose peat-free compost.

exam.q: Explain why high biodiversity is important for an ecosystem.
ms: Greater stability of the ecosystem.
Species are less dependent on any single species for food/shelter.

exam.q: Explain how deforestation of tropical rainforest can contribute to global warming and reduce biodiversity.
ms: Trees burnt release carbon dioxide.
Decay of felled trees by microorganisms releases carbon dioxide.
Fewer trees so less CO₂ removed by photosynthesis.
Higher CO₂ increases greenhouse effect/global warming.
Habitats destroyed so species lose food and shelter.
Replaced by monoculture crops/cattle, reducing variety of species.

example.title: Explaining eutrophication
example.q: Explain why fish die when fertiliser runs off into a pond.
steps: Nitrates cause algae to grow rapidly on the surface.
Algae block light, so plants below cannot photosynthesise and die.
Decomposing bacteria respire and use up dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate.

lessons.title: Climate and maintaining biodiversity
lessons.summary: Increasing greenhouse gases contribute to higher global temperature.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Increasing greenhouse gases contribute to higher global temperature. Changing climate can alter distribution, migration and food availability and increase extinction risk. Distinguish long-term trends from daily weather, and consider uncertainty and time span when interpreting evidence.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Breeding programmes, protected habitats, restoration, hedgerows and field margins can support biodiversity. Reducing deforestation, emissions and waste can reduce damage. Compare ecological benefits with cost, housing or food-production needs to make a reasoned judgement.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Biological consequences of global warming. Loss of habitat when low-lying areas flood; changes in distribution as species move to cooler areas; changes in migration patterns; reduced biodiversity; spread of pests and diseases into new regions.

Programmes to protect biodiversity. Breeding programmes for endangered species; protection and regeneration of rare habitats; reintroduction of field margins and hedgerows where there is monoculture; reduction of deforestation and carbon emissions; recycling instead of landfill.

Conflicting pressures. Protecting biodiversity can conflict with needs for food, housing, jobs and income; conservation can cost money; monitoring is needed.

keypoints: Increasing greenhouse gases contribute to higher global temperature.
Breeding programmes, protected habitats, restoration, hedgerows and field margins can support biodiversity.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Which supports habitat connectivity?
Why does one cold day not disprove warming?
opts: Weather varies while climate uses long-term data
checks.why: Weather varies while climate uses long-term data

checks.q: Which can maintain biodiversity on farms?
Why might species move further north as climate warms?
opts: Their original range becomes too warm

checks.q: A breeding programme helps conservation by…
Why can conservation conflict with human needs?
opts: Land is also needed for food and housing

exam.q: Evaluate restoring wetland on agricultural land.
ms: It can restore habitats and biodiversity / carbon storage.
It may reduce agricultural land or income.
A judgement should weigh local ecological benefit against food and cost implications.

exam.q: Give two ways people could reduce the effect of global warming on biodiversity.
ms: Reduce carbon emissions / burn fewer fossil fuels.
Reduce deforestation / plant trees / protect habitats.

exam.q: Explain how global warming could affect the distribution of species and biodiversity.
ms: Higher temperatures make some areas unsuitable.
Species move to cooler areas / higher latitudes or altitudes.
Migration patterns change / habitats lost as sea levels rise.
Species unable to move or adapt may become extinct, reducing biodiversity.

example.title: Evaluating a scheme
example.q: The government pays farmers to plant field margins. Evaluate the scheme.
steps: Margins provide habitats and food for insects and birds, and links between habitats.
Less land for crops, so lower income without the payment.
Worthwhile if payments cover losses and monitoring shows biodiversity increases.

lessons.title: Decomposition, compost and biogas
lessons.summary: Decomposer activity depends on moisture, oxygen and temperature.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Decomposer activity depends on moisture, oxygen and temperature. Warming increases enzyme activity up to an optimum; excessive heat denatures enzymes. Aerating compost supports aerobic decomposition, returning useful nutrients to soil.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Milk decay can be followed through falling pH as microorganisms produce acids. Compare time for a defined change at controlled temperatures. Anaerobic decay in biogas generators produces methane fuel. A pH-change rate is a proxy, not a direct bacterial count.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Required practical: temperature and milk decay. Mix milk, sodium carbonate solution (alkaline) and lipase in a test tube with phenolphthalein indicator, which is pink in alkali. At set temperatures in water baths, time how long the pink colour takes to disappear as lipase breaks fats into fatty acids, lowering pH. Rate = 1000 ÷ time.

Compost. Gardeners provide warm, moist, aerated conditions so decomposers work quickly and make compost to use as fertiliser.

Biogas. Anaerobic decay produces methane. Biogas generators can run on animal waste and plant material; the gas is burnt for heating or electricity, and the remaining slurry is a fertiliser.

keypoints: Decomposer activity depends on moisture, oxygen and temperature.
Milk decay can be followed through falling pH as microorganisms produce acids.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: A fixed pH change takes 40 min. Calculate 1/time.
Why turn compost?
Which indicator is used in the milk decay practical?
What gas is produced in a biogas generator?
Why does the pH of decaying milk fall?
Which condition slows decay?

exam.q: Why can decay be slow in both cold and very hot conditions?
ms: Cold reduces enzyme-controlled reaction rates.
Very high heat denatures enzymes / kills decomposers.
Both reduce microbial breakdown of biological material.

exam.q: Explain why compost heaps should be turned regularly.
ms: Turning adds oxygen.
For aerobic respiration by decomposers, which speeds decay.

exam.q: Describe how to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of milk.
ms: Add milk, sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein to a test tube.
Place tubes of milk and lipase in a water bath at set temperature to equilibrate.
Add lipase, start stopwatch.
Record time for pink colour to disappear.
Repeat at different temperatures, e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50 °C.
Calculate rate = 1000/time; keep volumes the same and repeat.

practical.title: Required practical 10 · Temperature and milk decay
method: Use the teacher-approved milk preparation with a suitable pH measurement method.
Hold samples at controlled temperatures and measure pH at regular intervals or time to a fixed pH change.
Repeat at each temperature with equal starting conditions.
variables: Independent: temperature.
Dependent: pH-change rate or reciprocal endpoint time.
Control milk composition, volume, starting pH and microorganism source.
safety: Never taste samples; avoid contact with cultures.
Follow school biological-waste disposal and hot-water-bath procedures.
practical.analysis: Compare means and uncertainty. Acid production causes the pH fall; this is a proxy for decay, not a direct count of all microorganisms.

example.title: Comparing rates
example.q: The pink colour disappears in 400 s at 20 °C and 160 s at 35 °C. Calculate both rates and compare.
steps: The rate at 35 °C is 2.5 times faster as enzymes have more kinetic energy.

lessons.title: Trophic levels and biomass efficiency
lessons.summary: Producers occupy trophic level 1 followed by primary, secondary and tertiary consumers.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Producers occupy trophic level 1 followed by primary, secondary and tertiary consumers. Biomass pyramids compare dry mass at a stated time. Less biomass reaches higher levels because not all is eaten, some is undigested and respiration releases carbon dioxide.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Efficiency = biomass transferred ÷ biomass available × 100. A transfer of 600 kg from 8000 kg is 7.5%. Energy transfers to surroundings rather than being destroyed. Do not assume every ecosystem has the same efficiency or confuse dry biomass with organism number.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Why biomass is lost between levels. Not all ingested material is absorbed — some is egested as faeces. Some absorbed material is lost as waste such as CO₂ and water from respiration, and urea in urine. Large amounts of glucose are used in respiration. Only about 10% of biomass is typically passed on.

Drawing a pyramid. Draw bars to scale, with producers at the bottom. Width represents biomass, not number.

Implications. Food chains rarely have more than four or five levels; eating plants directly is more efficient than eating animals that ate plants.

keypoints: Producers occupy trophic level 1 followed by primary, secondary and tertiary consumers.
Efficiency = biomass transferred ÷ biomass available × 100.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: 50 kg transfers from a level with 500 kg. Calculate efficiency.
Which reduces biomass available to the next level?
Producers have 10 000 kg; primary consumers 900 kg. Efficiency?
Which is NOT a reason biomass is lost?
A pyramid of biomass is usually pyramid-shaped because…
opts: less biomass is at each higher level
it is drawn that way by convention only

checks.q: Why are food chains rarely longer than five levels?
opts: Too little biomass remains for higher levels
checks.why: Losses at each level limit chain length.

exam.q: Explain decreasing biomass at higher trophic levels.
ms: Some material is not eaten.
Some eaten material is not digested and is egested.
Respiration releases carbon dioxide and transfers energy to surroundings.

exam.q: Explain why a pyramid of biomass is a better representation than a pyramid of numbers.
ms: A single large producer (e.g. a tree) can support many consumers, giving odd-shaped number pyramids.
Biomass takes account of the mass of organisms / shows the amount of material at each level.

exam.q: Explain why only a small proportion of the biomass at one trophic level is transferred to the next.
ms: Not all the organism is eaten, e.g. roots, bones.
Some material is egested as faeces / not digested.
Much glucose is used in respiration, releasing CO₂ and water.
Some is lost in waste, e.g. urea in urine.

example.title: Efficiency calculation
example.q: Grass contains 12 000 kg of biomass; rabbits contain 1080 kg; foxes contain 90 kg. Calculate both efficiencies.
steps: Less than 10% of biomass is passed on at each level.

lessons.title: Food security and sustainable production
lessons.summary: Food security means access to sufficient safe nutritious food.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Food security means access to sufficient safe nutritious food. Population growth, climate, pests, disease, conflict and costs influence supply and access. Fishing quotas and suitable net sizes allow populations to reproduce. Increased production alone does not guarantee fair distribution.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Controlled livestock conditions can reduce energy used in movement and warming but raise welfare concerns. Fermenters produce fungal mycoprotein; modified crops may improve nutrition or resistance. Evaluate output, resource use, emissions, welfare and cost rather than assuming a single solution works everywhere.

notes.title: Mycoprotein and improved nutrition
notes.html: Fusarium fungus can grow aerobically on a carbohydrate feed in a fermenter, supplying protein-rich food. Controlled oxygen, temperature and nutrient supply support growth; harvested biomass is processed for food. Genetically modified crops can also improve nutritional content, such as enhanced vitamin precursors, but suitability depends on the dietary problem and local evidence.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Threats to food security. Increasing birth rate; changing diets in developed countries; new pests and pathogens; environmental changes such as drought; cost of agricultural inputs; conflicts.

Increasing efficiency. Limiting movement and keeping animals warm reduces energy transferred to the environment, so more biomass becomes meat. Some people see this as cruel; animals may be fed high-protein food.

Sustainable fisheries. Quotas limit the number of fish caught; net mesh size lets young fish escape to breed.

Biotechnology. Mycoprotein from Fusarium is grown on glucose syrup in aerobic fermenters and purified into protein-rich food. GM crops can increase yields or nutrition.

keypoints: Food security means access to sufficient safe nutritious food.
Controlled livestock conditions can reduce energy used in movement and warming but raise welfare concerns.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Which can support sustainable fishing?
Why can restricted movement increase livestock growth?
opts: Less energy is used in movement
checks.why: Less energy is used in movement

checks.q: What is mycoprotein made from?
What do fishing quotas do?
opts: Limit the number of fish caught

checks.q: Why are intensively farmed animals kept warm?
opts: Less energy is used to maintain body temperature

checks.q: Which is a threat to food security?

exam.q: Evaluate intensive indoor livestock production.
ms: Controlled temperature / movement can increase growth efficiency.
Welfare, disease or resource-use concerns must be considered.
A justified judgement weighs food yield against costs and alternatives.

exam.q: Explain why limiting the movement of farm animals increases food production efficiency.
ms: Less energy is transferred in movement/respiration.
So more biomass/energy is stored as body tissue/meat.

exam.q: Describe how mycoprotein is produced and evaluate its use as a food.
ms: Fusarium grown in aerobic fermenter on glucose syrup.
Conditions (temperature, pH, oxygen) controlled; mycoprotein harvested and purified.
Benefit: high protein, low fat; less land and fewer emissions than meat.
Limitation: needs energy/glucose feed; some people may dislike taste/processing.

example.title: Why net size matters
example.q: Explain how increasing the mesh size of fishing nets helps cod populations recover.
steps: Small, young fish pass through the larger holes.
They survive to reach breeding age.
More young are produced, so the population can increase.

Placing quadrats where there are most plants.

In grass → rabbit → fox, the fox is a…

Why do extremophiles survive in hot springs?

Place quadrats at coordinates and count clover in each.
Use many quadrats (e.g. 10+) and calculate the mean.

ms: Microorganisms decompose dead organisms and waste.
They respire, releasing CO₂ into the atmosphere.
CO₂ is then taken in by plants in photosynthesis.

exam.q: Explain how human activities reduce biodiversity and describe ways biodiversity can be maintained.
